sentences.text: Gnatusuchus possessed highly reduced dentition, featuring only fourteen upper teeth and eleven lower teeth, far fewer than the eighteen to twenty found in other blunt-snouted caimans.
The front teeth were long, peg-like, and procumbent, showing signs of wear on their tips.
In contrast, the rear teeth were globular in shape with a distinct neck.
Based on skull measurements, researchers estimate the animal reached a total body length between 148.9 and 167.7 centimeters.
The genus name Gnatusuchus combines the Quechua word for 'small nose' and the Greek word for 'crocodile'.
This creature lived in the Pebas mega-wetlands, a vast system covering over one million square kilometers in modern-day Peru.
Gnatusuchus pebasensis was named in 2015 based on a nearly complete skull and several jaws found in the Pebas Formation near Iquitos in Peru.
The holotype of Gnatusuchus is a nearly complete skull (MUSM 990) found in the Iquitos area of Peru, accompanied by three partial mandible specimens.
The youngest fossil records of Gnatusuchus come from the Nueva Unión area south of Iquitos, Peru.
Researchers hypothesize that Gnatusuchus used its front teeth to shovel food while crushing bivalve shells with its tightly packed rear teeth.
Gnatusuchus is classified within the family Alligatoridae and belongs to the subfamily Caimaninae.
Phylogenetic analysis places Gnatusuchus as the most basal member of the Caimaninae subfamily, and it is a member of the class Reptilia.
Gnatusuchus lived during the Langhian to Serravallian stages, from 15.98 to 11.63 million years ago.
It is noted that Gnatusuchus has not been found in the Urumaco or Solimões formations where other durophagous caimans persisted after the Pebas wetlands declined.
